463.title: The Friday surah
463.hook: many read al-Kahf every Friday, a practice drawn from hadith (Hakim; Bayhaqi)
463.tomorrow: The young men in the cave
463.howItsDone: Many Muslims read Surat al-Kahf every Friday, or from Thursday sunset, alone or in groups at the mosque; some also memorize its first ten verses, following the hadith in Sahih Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dawn recitation, and your line was dawn is witnessed. Did you say your line this morning before the phone? What was the quiet like? Day four hundred sixty-three, and a new surah.

A Friday morning, a mosque, an hour before the noon prayer. Along the walls, people sit alone, each with a Qur'an open to the same place. Ask one of them and you may hear: it's Friday, so it's al-Kahf. Surah eighteen. The Cave. A surah with a weekly appointment. Some read it in Arabic, some in translation, some under their breath. Today, before we open its stories, where that appointment comes from.

The custom rests on a hadith recorded by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi: whoever reads Surat al-Kahf on Friday, a light will shine for them between the two Fridays. A week of light, from one reading to the next. Hadith scholars have discussed how strong its chains are, and the practice has lasted. Because the Islamic day begins at sunset, some read it on Thursday night, others on Friday itself. Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, says that whoever memorizes the first ten verses of al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjal, the great deceiver of the end of time. That's one reason some families teach those ten verses early. And Bukhari tells a scene: a companion was reciting al-Kahf at night, his horse tied nearby, and a cloud came down over him and began to circle; the horse grew restless. In the morning he told the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who said: that was the sakinah, the tranquility, which came down for the Qur'an. The surah opens, in Pickthall's words: "Praise be to Allah Who hath revealed the Scripture unto His slave, and hath not placed therein any crookedness". Then come four long stories: young men who hide in a cave, a man with two gardens, Musa traveling to learn from a stranger, and a powerful traveler who builds a wall. Some teachers today read them as four trials: of faith, of wealth, of knowledge, and of power. That framing is a modern reading, not a hadith, but it helps hold the surah in your head. For the next week, we'll walk through it, one story at a time.

segments.voice: The practice is to plan to read it this Friday. Sit, and think through your coming Friday. Where's a half hour that could belong to al-Kahf? Before work, at lunch, after the noon prayer, on the train. If the whole surah feels like a lot, plan for the first ten, in Arabic or in translation. Picture where you'll sit and what the page will look like. If you pray, you can ask for that week of light. The bell holds the time.

464.title: The young men in the cave
464.word: The young men in the cave
464.hook: young believers flee to a cave and pray, our Lord, grant us mercy and set right our affair (18:10)
464.howItsDone: The du'a of 18:10 is memorized by Muslims and said in Arabic when facing a difficult situation; it's also recited as part of al-Kahf on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Friday surah, al-Kahf, and your line was friday's surah. Is it in your calendar yet, with a time and a place? Day four hundred sixty-four.

A handful of young men in a city where their faith has become dangerous. Their people, the surah says, have taken other gods beside the One. They can stay and pretend, or they can go. They go. Out past the edge of town, up into the hills, into a cave in the rock, with nothing but each other and a dog. And the first thing they do, once they're inside and the noise is gone, is ask for something. Today: what they ask.

The Qur'an calls them fitya, young men, youths. Verse thirteen says they believed in their Lord, and God increased them in guidance. Verse fourteen says God bound their hearts firm when they stood up and said: our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Then they withdrew. And at the cave mouth, in Pickthall's translation of verse ten: "Our Lord! Give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight." Look at the two halves. Mercy from Your presence: min ladunk, from with You, straight from God rather than from the people around them. And then: arrange for us, out of our affair, rashad, right guidance, a sound way through. They don't ask to win. They don't ask for their enemies to fall. They ask for mercy and for their situation to be set straight. What happens next is that God puts them to sleep, which we'll come to tomorrow. The Qur'an doesn't name the city or the century. It mentions ar-Raqim, a word commentators explain in different ways: an inscribed tablet, a place, a valley. Christians tell a story of sleepers in a cave near Ephesus, and some Muslim commentators connected the two; the Qur'an itself leaves the details open, and warns, a few verses on, against arguing about them. What it keeps is the prayer. Muslims still say it, word for word in Arabic, when a situation is beyond them: rabbana atina min ladunka rahmah, wa hayyi' lana min amrina rashada. It's the prayer of people who've done the one thing they could do, which was to leave, and hand the rest over.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one situation in your life that's tangled: a job, a family knot, a decision with no clean answer. Picture yourself stepping out of it for two minutes, the way they stepped into the cave. Let the noise drop. If you pray, you can say their du'a, in Arabic or in your own language: our Lord, give us mercy from Your presence, and set right our affair. If you don't, just hold the situation without trying to fix it, and let it be held. The bell holds the time.

465.title: The dog at the threshold
465.hook: they sleep for years with their dog stretched at the entrance (18:18, 18:25)
465.howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of the man who watered a thirsty dog when teaching kindness to animals; schools of law differ on the ritual purity of dogs and on keeping them indoors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the young men in the cave, and their prayer. Your line was set right our affair. Did you do your one part and let go of the rest? Day four hundred sixty-five.

The young men have prayed, and now they sleep. Inside the cave it's dim. The sun, the surah says, swings past the opening, to the right in the morning and the left in the evening, so it never falls full on them. Someone looking in would swear they were awake. And lying across the entrance, front legs stretched out on the threshold, is a dog. The Qur'an tells you exactly where it lies.

Verse eighteen, in Pickthall's words, ends: "and their dog stretching out his paws on the threshold." Al-wasid, the threshold, the open ground at the mouth of the cave. The dog is lying where a guard would lie. In the same verse, God turns the sleepers over, to the right and to the left, while the dog stays where it is. Then, a few verses on, the story does something unusual. People argue about how many sleepers there were. Some will say three, their dog the fourth. Some say five, their dog the sixth, guessing at the unseen. Some say seven, and their dog the eighth. And the verse ends: say, my Lord knows best their number. Notice: nobody's count leaves out the dog. The men are a number in dispute; the dog is in every version. Verse twenty-five gives a length for the sleep, three hundred years and nine more, and the next verse adds that God knows best how long they stayed. And the animal that followed them in is remembered in a surah recited on Fridays. There's a hadith in Bukhari that fits beside it. A man walking on a hot road found a dog panting and licking the dirt from thirst. He climbed down into a well, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth to climb back up, and gave the dog a drink. God thanked him and forgave him. The companions asked: is there reward for us even with animals? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: in every living, breathing creature there is reward. Muslim schools of law differ about dogs, their purity and keeping them in the house. On kindness to them, the hadith is plain.

segments.voice: The practice is to be kind to a dog, and if there's no dog nearby, to any animal. Sit, and bring to mind an animal you know: a neighbor's dog, a cat on a wall, the pigeons at the bus stop. Picture what it needs: water on a hot day, shade, someone not shooing it. Think of one small, safe kindness you could do for it, or for animals like it, this week. A bowl of water by the door counts. The bell holds the time.

466.title: Say inshallah
466.hook: never say I'll do it tomorrow without, if Allah wills (18:23–24)
466.howItsDone: Muslims say inshallah when speaking of any future plan, following 18:23–24; many scholars teach that it should accompany a sincere intention, and that if forgotten, it can be said on remembering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dog at the threshold, and your line was even the dog is remembered. Did an animal get a kindness from you? Day four hundred sixty-six.

See you at eight, inshallah. The test is Thursday, inshallah. We'll finish the kitchen by spring, inshallah. If you have Muslim friends or coworkers, you've heard it tacked onto plans so often it sounds like punctuation. Some people even joke that it's a polite way of saying probably not. But the word comes from the middle of al-Kahf, right in between the story of the cave and the story of the gardens, and it arrived, the biographies say, after an awkward silence.

Here's the story as Ibn Ishaq's biography tells it. It's from the sirah, not from the Qur'an or the major hadith collections. The Quraysh in Mecca put three questions to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: about young men who disappeared long ago, about a great traveler, and about the spirit. He said: I'll tell you tomorrow. He didn't add: if God wills. And tomorrow came, and no revelation. Nor the next day. By this account the wait lasted around fifteen days, and the people of Mecca mocked him. When the answer came, it included this, in Pickthall's words: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." In Arabic: in sha' Allah. If God wills. Three words that became one. Notice what the verse is doing. It's not banning plans. You're still meant to say I'll do it tomorrow. It's adding the honest clause: the future isn't in your hands. Every plan you make is made inside a will larger than yours. Then the verse goes on: remember your Lord when you forget. In other words, if you made a plan and forgot to say it, say it when you remember. No penalty, no guilt, just come back. And the end of the verse: say, perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right than this. So inshallah isn't meant to be a polite no. Scholars have long said it should go with a real intention to do the thing. It's a yes, held with open hands.

segments.voice: Sit, and run through your plans for tomorrow: the meetings, the errands, the call you've been meaning to make. As each one comes up, add the clause. If you're Muslim, inshallah. If not, you can try the plain meaning: if it's given to me. Notice how each plan feels with that clause attached. Lighter? Less certain? More honest? Don't drop any plans. Just hold each one a little more loosely. The bell holds the time.

Your line: if allah wills. Today, add it to every plan you make, aloud or silently, and mean the plan. Day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: Two gardens
467.hook: a rich man boasts of his gardens, and they are ruined overnight (18:32–43)
467.howItsDone: Muslims say mashallah when admiring a blessing, their own or someone else's, often adding la quwwata illa billah; some also say it to ward off envy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: say inshallah, and your line was if Allah wills. Did you attach it to a plan, and mean the plan? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

Two men. One of them owns two vineyards, hedged around with date palms, fields of grain between them, a stream running through the middle. Both gardens bear fruit and hold nothing back. The other man has much less. The rich man starts talking to his friend, and then walks into his garden, still talking. Al-Kahf calls this a parable, a story set out as an example. Today: what he says in that garden, and what his friend says back.

The rich man says three things, and each one goes further. First: I have more than you in wealth, and more people behind me. That's comparison. Then, walking into his garden, the surah says he wrongs himself and says: I don't think this will ever perish. That's permanence. Then: and I don't think the Hour will ever come, and even if I'm brought back to my Lord, I'll find something better there. That's entitlement. His friend doesn't mock him. He answers: do you deny the One who made you from dust? And then he gives the line this day is built on. In Pickthall's translation: "If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah!" In Arabic: ma sha' Allah, la quwwata illa billah. What God wills. There is no power except through God. Yesterday's word was inshallah, if God wills, said about the future. Today's is mashallah, what God has willed, said about what's already here. One is for plans. The other is for blessings. Then the story ends quickly. The fruit is struck. The man stands in his garden wringing his hands over everything he spent on it, the vines collapsed on their trellises, and he says: I wish I had not set anything beside my Lord. Today mashallah is said when admiring something: a new baby, a friend's house, a child's grades, and some say it as protection against envy. But in al-Kahf its first job is simpler: to remember, out loud, whose the garden was.

segments.voice: Your own garden: the things you're proud of. A home, a skill, a body that works, children, a paycheck, a reputation. Walk through it in your mind, slowly, the way the rich man walked through his. At each thing, pause. If you're Muslim, you can say mashallah, la quwwata illa billah. If not, simply notice: I didn't make this alone. Then stay with whatever feeling comes, gratitude, or worry about losing it. The bell holds the time.

Your line: mashallah, no power but his. Today, when you admire something, yours or someone else's, say it, and remember whose it is. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: Musa meets al-Khidr
468.hook: Musa travels to learn from a servant given knowledge, and promises patience (18:65–70)
468.carry: you won't be able to be patient
468.tomorrow: The boat, the boy, the wall
468.howItsDone: Muslim teachers use the story of Musa and al-Khidr to teach the manners of learning: humility before a teacher, patience, and not presuming one knows the most; it is read with all of al-Kahf on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two gardens, and your line was mashallah, no power but His. When you admired something, did you remember whose it was? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

Musa has stood before Pharaoh, crossed the sea, received the Torah. And in a hadith in Bukhari, someone asks him: who is the most knowledgeable person on earth? He says: I am. God corrects him. There is a servant of Mine, at the place where the two seas meet, who knows more than you. So the great teacher packs a bag and goes looking for a teacher, one who will not let him ask questions.
screen: `THE TEACHER GOES LOOKING FOR A TEACHER.`

segments.voice: In the hadith, God tells Musa to carry a fish in a basket: where you lose the fish, you'll find him. Musa sets out with a young servant, named Yusha' in the hadith. At a rock by the sea they rest, and the fish slips into the water and swims off, leaving a strange tunnel in the sea. The young man forgets to mention it. Later, tired and hungry, Musa asks for their meal, and the young man remembers. Musa says: that's the place we were looking for. They retrace their steps. And there, the Qur'an says, they find one of Our servants, to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our presence. The Qur'an never names him. The hadith calls him al-Khidr, the green one, because, it says, where he sat on bare ground, it turned green. Musa asks, very politely: may I follow you, so that you teach me some of the right guidance you've been taught? And the answer, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! thou canst not bear with me." Then: how could you be patient with what you can't fully understand? Look at Musa's reply. He says, in sha' Allah, you will find me patient, and I won't disobey you in anything. This week's two words, inshallah and mashallah, are still in the air. Al-Khidr sets one condition: if you follow me, don't ask me about anything until I bring it up myself. Musa, a prophet who spoke with God, agrees to be a student who keeps quiet. That's the lesson before any of the lessons. The man who answered I am, when asked who knew the most, still had something to learn, and he was willing to walk to find it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you don't usually learn from. Someone younger, or with less schooling, or from a job you overlook, or someone you disagree with. Picture them clearly. Now ask: what do they know that I don't? Maybe how to fix something, how to be calm, how to live on less. Let the answer come slowly. Then imagine yourself asking them about it, and, like Musa, keeping quiet long enough to actually hear the answer. The bell holds the time.
Musa meets al-Khidr. A great prophet becomes a student, walks to the meeting of two seas, and promises a patience he's told he won't have. Today's word.

469.title: The boat, the boy, the wall
469.hook: each strange act has a hidden mercy Musa couldn't see (18:71–82)
469.howItsDone: Muslims read 18:71–82 as a lesson in trusting God's wisdom in hardship, while scholars stress that al-Khidr's acts were by special divine command and are never a precedent for anyone to cause harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Musa meets al-Khidr, and the warning: you won't be able to be patient. Did you learn something from someone unexpected? Day four hundred sixty-nine, the end of a week.
screen: `YOU WON'T BE ABLE TO BE PATIENT.`

segments.voice: Musa has promised to ask nothing. They set off along the shore. A boat's crew recognizes al-Khidr and lets them both ride for free. And the moment they're aboard, al-Khidr takes a tool and knocks a hole in the boat. Musa forgets his promise in a heartbeat: you've made a hole to drown its people? Al-Khidr says, quietly: didn't I tell you you couldn't be patient? That's the first of three. Today: all three, and what was behind them.

Musa apologizes: don't blame me for forgetting. They go on. They meet a boy, and al-Khidr kills him. Musa is horrified, and says so: you've killed an innocent soul. Second warning. They come to a town, hungry, and ask for food. The people refuse them. In that same town there's a wall about to fall down, and al-Khidr rebuilds it. Musa says: you could at least have charged them for it. And al-Khidr says: this is where we part. Then he explains. The boat belonged to poor people who worked the sea, and a king ahead was seizing every sound boat by force. A damaged boat would be left alone. The boy, he says, would have pressed his believing parents into rebellion and disbelief, and God would give them a better child in his place. The wall stood over a treasure belonging to two orphan boys whose father had been a righteous man, and God wanted them to grow up and dig it out themselves. And then the line, in Pickthall's words: "I did it not upon my own command." Muslim scholars are clear about the second scene: al-Khidr acted on direct command from God, about a future only God knew, and no person may take it as permission for harm. The law forbids it. The story isn't teaching people to act on hidden reasons. It's teaching what it's like to watch from inside a story you can't see the end of. Bukhari's hadith adds two details: a small bird dipped its beak in the sea, and al-Khidr said their knowledge beside God's was like that sip beside the ocean. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: we wish Musa had been patient, so we could have been told more. This week ran from the Friday surah through the cave, the dog, inshallah, the gardens, and now this: a reason under the surface.
screen: `THE BOAT: A KING WHO SEIZES SHIPS.` · `THE BOY: A FUTURE ONLY GOD KNEW.` · `THE WALL: TWO ORPHANS' TREASURE.` · `A BIRD'S SIP FROM THE SEA.` · then, large: `I DID IT NOT UPON MY OWN COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a setback from your past, something that felt like a hole knocked in your boat: a job you didn't get, a move you didn't want, a door that shut. Now, with some years between you and it, look again. Is there anything that came because of it, something you couldn't see at the time? If you find one, hold it. If you don't, that's honest too: some reasons stay hidden. The bell holds the time.
The boat. Holed to save it from a king, the first of three acts that looked wrong to Musa and turned out to hide a mercy. Today's word.
Your line: there was a reason. Today, when something small goes wrong, wait a little before deciding what it means. Day four hundred sixty-nine.

fork.setup: a town has refused you food. you see their wall about to collapse, and your companion rebuilds it for free. what do you say, as Musa?
options: thank him for his kindness.
you could at least have charged them for it.
help him build.
fork.reveal: Musa says he could have taken a wage, his third question, and al-Khidr says: this is where we part. then he explains all three.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason.
what it means: Musa watched three acts that looked wrong, and each held a mercy he couldn't see, yet nobody else is licensed to act on hidden reasons.
what a scholar hears: al-Khidr says 'I wanted' for the boat, 'we wanted' for the boy and 'your Lord wanted' for the wall; commentators read meaning in the shift.
